html:
A writing system for the Cherokee language, completed in 1821 by Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith who could not read or write any language. It has 85 symbols, each standing for a syllable.

Sequoyah had seen white men read and wanted the same power for his people. After years of trial, he showed his system to Cherokee leaders by having his young daughter read a message he had written out of her hearing. The Cherokee Nation adopted it in 1825.

Because each sign matched a sound speakers already knew, people learned it in days. Within a few years many Cherokee could read and write in their own language. In 1828 the nation began printing a newspaper, the Cherokee Phoenix, in Cherokee and English.

It is one of the very few times one person invented a full writing system from nothing, like the Korean hangul made by a royal team. The new literacy did not save the Cherokee from the Trail of Tears a decade later, but the script is still used today.
